subQuestions.questionText: Costs of inputs that are owned by an entrepreneur and used during the production process are regarded as … costs.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D – implicit (2 marks)
Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of using resources owned by the entrepreneur (e.g. own buildings, own labour) for which no direct monetary payment is made.

subQuestions.questionText: A market structure where there are no barriers to entry is called a/an … market.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A – perfect (or D – monopolistic competitive, both accepted) (2 marks)
A perfect (and monopolistic competitive) market has free entry and exit, with no barriers preventing new firms from entering.

subQuestions.questionText: When one dominant firm changes the price and others follow, it is regarded as price …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A – leadership (2 marks)
Price leadership occurs in oligopolies where one dominant firm sets the price and other firms follow.

subQuestions.questionText: Collusion is an agreement among firms to … competition.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D – limit (2 marks)
Collusion is an agreement among firms (often in an oligopoly) to limit competition by fixing prices, output, or market share.

subQuestions.questionText: A condition of low economic growth, high unemployment and high rates of inflation, is called …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C – stagflation (2 marks)
Stagflation describes the simultaneous combination of stagnant economic growth, high unemployment, and high inflation.

subQuestions.questionText: The site that boasts five different eco-systems:
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B – iSimangaliso Wetland Park (2 marks)
iSimangaliso Wetland Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in KwaZulu-Natal famous for containing five distinct ecosystems.

subQuestions.questionText: Cost-push inflation could be the result of …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B – depreciation of the currency (2 marks)
Depreciation of the currency increases the cost of imported inputs (e.g. oil), pushing up production costs and causing cost-push inflation.

subQuestions.questionText: A global problem that impacts the variation in weather patterns, is known as …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C – climate change (2 marks)
Climate change is a global environmental issue that affects long-term variations in weather patterns worldwide.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Cost-benefit analysis (Choose a description from COLUMN B that matches the item in COLUMN A. Options: A) people travelling through South Africa to another country; B) resources allocated in such a way that no one is made better off without making someone else worse off; C) an instrument used by the government to evaluate public projects; D) dumping of harmful substances into rivers; E) occurs when the aggregate demand for goods and services exceeds the aggregate supply of goods and services, leading to price increases; F) exists because of barriers to entry which are not economic in nature; G) decrease in average cost of production per unit as output increases; H) output sacrificed due to underutilisation of resources; I) increase in output with the same factor inputs)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C – an instrument used by the government to evaluate public projects (1 mark)
Cost-benefit analysis is used by government to weigh the costs and benefits of public projects to decide whether to proceed.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Artificial monopoly
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: F – exists because of barriers to entry which are not economic in nature (1 mark)
Artificial monopolies arise from non-economic barriers (such as legal/government restrictions, patents, or licences).

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Economies of scale
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: G – decrease in average cost of production per unit as output increases (1 mark)
Economies of scale occur when long-run average cost falls as a firm increases its scale of output.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Pareto efficiency
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B – resources allocated in such a way that no one is made better off without making someone else worse off (1 mark)
Pareto efficiency is a state of allocation where it is impossible to improve one party's welfare without harming another's.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Transit tourist
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A – people travelling through South Africa to another country (1 mark)
A transit tourist passes through a country en route to a final destination elsewhere.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Water pollution
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D – dumping of harmful substances into rivers (1 mark)
Water pollution involves the contamination of water bodies (rivers, oceans) by harmful substances.

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Productivity
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: I – increase in output with the same factor inputs (1 mark)
Productivity refers to producing more output without an increase in inputs (i.e. more efficient use of resources).

subQuestions.questionText: Match: Demand-pull inflation
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: E – occurs when the aggregate demand for goods and services exceeds the aggregate supply of goods and services, leading to price increases (1 mark)
Demand-pull inflation arises from excess aggregate demand relative to aggregate supply, pulling prices upward.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A market structure where firms use different types of packaging to market their products.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Monopolistic competition (1 mark)
Under monopolistic competition, firms differentiate similar products through packaging, branding, and advertising.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A situation where firms are allowed by law to charge prices above the market equilibrium price.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Price floor / minimum price (1 mark)
A price floor (minimum price) is a legal limit set above the equilibrium price, often to protect producers (e.g. minimum wage, agricultural support prices).

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A period where at least one factor of production is fixed.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Short-run (1 mark)
In the short-run, at least one factor of production (typically capital) is fixed while others can vary.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: The direct regulation of an industry or activity through laws that state what is allowed and what is illegal regarding pollution.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Command and control (1 mark)
Command and control measures are direct regulations imposed by government to limit pollution (e.g. legal emission limits, bans).

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: Financial support by the government to assist the production of a good or service.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Subsidy on production (1 mark)
A production subsidy is government financial assistance to producers to lower their costs and encourage production.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: The granting of legal titles to the owners of land so that it can be taken care of.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Property rights (1 mark)
Property rights give owners legal title to land/resources, creating an incentive to look after and manage them sustainably.

subQuestions.questionText: Name any TWO examples of a perfect market structure.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct example (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
• Agricultural sector
• Stock exchange
• Foreign exchange market
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How do oligopolists benefit from forming a cartel?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response (1 x 2):
It enables them to fix prices / restrict competition / restrict supply / increase market power.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the cost/revenue graph showing MC, AC, AVC and AR/MR/P curves with reference points (Quantity 20, 50, 60, 85 and prices 30 and 50). Which curve is used to determine the supply of the firm? (Refer to the graph in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: MC (Marginal Cost) (1 mark)
The portion of the MC curve above AVC represents the firm's supply curve in a perfect market.

subQuestions.questionText: Identify the profit maximisation quantity. (Refer to the graph in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: 60 (1 mark)
Profit is maximised where MC = MR, which occurs at quantity 60 on the graph.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term marginal revenue.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
Marginal revenue refers to the extra amount of income gained by selling one more unit of production (the additional revenue from selling one additional unit of output).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: When will a firm in a perfect market shut down its operations?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct response:
A firm will shut down when it can no longer cover its variable costs (i.e. where MC = AVC, or when price falls to R30, or when AR < AVC).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Use the graph above to determine the type of profit made by this firm. Show ALL correct calculations. (Refer to the graph in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 4 marks for correct calculation and identification of profit type:

Method 1: Profit = TR − TC
= (50 × 60) − (50 × 60)
= 3000 − 3000
= 0
Therefore, the firm is making normal profit.

OR

Method 2: Profit = (AR − AC) × Q
= (R50 − R50) × 60
= 0
Therefore, the firm is making normal profit.

Mark allocation: 1 mark for formula, 2 marks for substitution and calculation, 1 mark for stating normal profit.

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the cartoon on monopolistic competition. Determine the nature of the product sold in this market structure. (Refer to the cartoon in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Differentiated / heterogeneous (1 mark)
Monopolistic competitors sell similar but differentiated products (e.g. branded coffee).

subQuestions.questionText: What type of profit is made by monopolistic competitors in the long run?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Normal profit (1 mark)
In the long run, free entry and exit drives monopolistic competitors to earn only normal profit.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term hybrid structure.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
Hybrid structure describes the fact that monopolistic competition is comprised of the characteristics of both perfect competition and monopoly.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why does a monopoly fail to achieve productive efficiency?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE well-explained point. Acceptable points:
• The monopolist produces output that is less than the desired output / it fails to minimise average cost.
• Inefficiency may occur since there is no competition.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How do oligopolists maintain their market share?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks). Acceptable points:
• Oligopolists extend shopping hours to encourage greater flexibility for households.
• Promoting online purchases, which makes it easier for customers to shop around without any additional cost / variety of goods available to make comparisons.
• Implementing product differentiation, products might slightly differ in terms of physical appearance, packaging, etc.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks for mere listing of facts.)

subQuestions.questionText: Using TR and TC curves, draw a correctly labelled graph to briefly explain how a firm in a perfect market maximises profit.
subQuestions.memoText:
Graph allocation (Max 4 marks):
• 1 mark – labelling of axes (Cost & Revenue on Y-axis, Quantity on X-axis) / break-even points
• 2 marks – profit maximisation point (where TR − TC is greatest, e.g. at 70 units)
• 1 mark – correctly drawn TR and TC curves

Explanation (Max 4 marks):
• The firm will earn maximum profit where the difference between TR and TC is the greatest (at 70 units).
• This is at 70 units at a price of R50.
• Any other quantity produced will result in lower profits (e.g. Q50), a loss (e.g. Q100), or break-even (Q20 / Q85).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 4 marks for graph; A maximum of 4 marks for explanation.)

subQuestions.questionText: Outline the challenges that the competition policy in South Africa face in achieving their goals.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained challenge). Challenges experienced by the competition policy include:
• Fines charged are too lenient and do not cover the costs suffered by consumers.
• Fines are too lenient to act as a deterrent to other businesses colluding, evident from the larger number of firms being investigated regularly.
• A lack of human resources results in some investigations or acts of collusion sometimes going undetected.
• Cases of restrictive practices take longer to investigate and lose merit in the process.
• Corruption and political interference/interests prevent some acts of collusion from being investigated properly.
• Some mergers and acquisitions only protect workers in the short term — eventually workers are retrenched.
• Artificial monopolies and other powerful businesses abuse their market power as the competition policy fails to create opportunities for new entrants.
• The monitoring measures to identify collusion practices are compromised due to a lack of information, as many investigations take place after a long period of collusion.
• The monitoring and enforcement of competition policies is difficult due to the vastness of areas.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks will be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: Name any TWO examples of sites in South Africa that promote cultural tourism.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct example (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
• Robben Island
• Table Mountain National Park
• Apartheid Museum
• Richtersveld Cultural and Botanical Landscape
• District Six
• Bo-Kaap
• Constitutional Hill
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: What is the negative impact of an increase in indirect taxes on goods and services?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response:
It will lead to higher prices of goods and services, which will decrease aggregate demand and slow down the economy.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the Monthly Consumer Price Index (CPI) Figures 2019–2020 graph. During which month in 2020 was the inflation rate outside the target range? (Refer to the graph in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: May / June (2020) (1 mark)
The SARB inflation target range is 3–6%. In May 2020 (1.2%) and June 2020 (2.2%), inflation fell below the lower limit of 3%.

subQuestions.questionText: Determine the increase in the inflation rate between June 2020 and July 2020. (Refer to the graph in the question paper.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: 1% (or 1 percentage point) (1 mark)
June 2020: 2.2% → July 2020: 3.2%, giving an increase of 3.2% − 2.2% = 1%.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term production price index.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
The production price index is an index that measures the prices of domestically produced goods and shows domestic output / measures prices of goods that are produced domestically when they leave the factory yard.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the reason for the exclusion of certain items from the CPI basket, when calculating core inflation.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct explanation:
Government excludes certain items, such as fresh/frozen food, because they have highly volatile prices. Goods that are affected by government intervention or policies (e.g. subsidies on bread) are also excluded to give a clearer view of underlying inflation.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How will an increase in social and unemployment grants influence inflation?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks). Acceptable points:
• Aggregate demand will increase for goods and services, thereby raising prices.
• Income levels for the poor and unemployed will increase, thereby increasing consumer spending.
• Creates an opportunity for producers to use the increase in social grants to increase their profit margins.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the extract on State of the Environment. Identify the concept related to the removal of trees.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Deforestation (1 mark)
Deforestation is the large-scale removal/clearing of trees and forests.

subQuestions.questionText: Name ONE organisation that campaigns for the sustainable use of the environment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark for any one of:
• World Wildlife Fund (WWF)
• Green Trust
• Collect-a-Can
• Keep South Africa Beautiful
• Greenpeace
• Friends of the Earth
• Rainforest Alliance
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term hazardous waste.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
Hazardous waste is waste products that take time to decompose / are dangerous or toxic to human and animal life.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the way in which the Convention on the International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) aims to reduce biodiversity loss.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE well-explained point. Acceptable points:
• CITES bans commercial international trade in endangered species.
• CITES uses permits and quotas to regulate and monitor trade in other species that may become endangered.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How can the government address the extinction of animal species?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks). Acceptable points:
• Community members should be educated on the dangers of killing animals.
• Encourage community members to report any activities related to illegal killing of animals by offering incentives.
• Grant property rights to private individuals and businesses to increase interest in preserving endangered animal species.
• Improve security in game reserves where most endangered animal species are located.
• Prohibit hunting activities in areas where animals threatened by extinction are located.
• Impose huge fines on those who are illegally hunting.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Discuss the negative effects of soil erosion on the environment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (4 x 2 = 8 marks). Acceptable points:
• Soil erosion occurs when the topsoil is removed through the action of wind and water at a greater rate than it is formed.
• It leads to increased pollution in streams and rivers.
• It is a major environmental threat to sustainability and productivity as it affects soil fertility and food security.
• It degrades land and often makes it less productive.
• Erosion may result in the destruction of water sources such as dams.
• It destroys the ecosystem (the grazing land for animals).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 4 marks will be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: How would low inflation expectations by the consumer keep inflation within the target range?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained point). Low inflation expectations:
• Limit excessive wage demands by different labour unions because workers do not expect increases in cost of living in the future.
• Allow consumers to postpone consumption expenditure, thereby reducing pressure on price increases.
• Give households confidence that the inflation rate will be low in future and encourage them to save more from their income, thereby controlling excess demand.
• Reduce panic buying by consumers when they expect that prices will be stable in the future.
• Boost real interest rates which will encourage savings.
• Increase the burden on debtors which discourages them from borrowing money, due to the higher real interest rate.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks will be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: Name any TWO major international agreements on sustainable development.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct example (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
• Rio de Janeiro (Earth Summit)
• Johannesburg Summit
• Kyoto Protocol
• COP 17
(Accept any other relevant and correct response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why do homogeneous products benefit consumers?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response:
Consumers are guaranteed standardised products because it allows them to buy from any seller (and they know what to expect in terms of quality).
(Accept any other relevant and correct response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the extract on Electricity Prices. Which type of monopoly is discussed in the extract above?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Natural monopoly / State-owned monopoly (1 mark)
Eskom is a natural/state-owned monopoly because of the high infrastructure costs and government ownership.

subQuestions.questionText: What determines the quantity sold by a monopoly?
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Market demand / revenue / cost (1 mark)
A monopoly determines its quantity sold based on the interaction of market demand, marginal revenue, and marginal cost.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term economic profit.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
Economic profit is achieved when total revenue is greater than total cost / average revenue is greater than average cost / profit that is made above (in addition to) normal profit.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the relatively inelastic nature of the demand curve for the monopolist.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for ONE well-explained point. Acceptable points:
• Monopolists sell unique products with no close substitutes / consumers have no other alternative options of goods and services.
• Competition is limited due to the unique nature of the product or huge capital needed to start the business.
(Accept any other relevant correct response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why is it difficult to enter into a monopoly market?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks). Acceptable points:
• Government sets restrictions which make it difficult for new firms to enter the monopoly industry.
• Strategic industries in the country need barriers to protect the market against penetration.
• High development cost (huge capital outlay) is needed to enter such a market.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(Max 2 marks for mere listing of facts.)

subQuestions.questionText: Refer to the information on Marketable Permits. Which government department is responsible for granting marketable permits?
subQuestions.memoText: Correct answer: Department of Mineral Resources and Energy (1 mark)

subQuestions.questionText: Name ONE market-related measure to protect the environment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark for any one of:
• Recycling
• Environmentally friendly products
• Technology
• Renewable energy
• Tradeable emissions permits
• Congestion charges
(Accept any other relevant correct answer.)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term marketable permits.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct definition:
A marketable permit is a license issued by the government to each business to pollute to a certain degree (and these permits can be traded between firms).
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the effect of carbon emissions on agricultural production.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct explanation:
Carbon emissions may result in acid rains or a change in climatic conditions which will destroy agricultural products thereby decreasing production.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How do green taxes contribute to the promotion of a more sustainable environment?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per well-explained point (2 x 2 = 4 marks). Acceptable points:
• Production of harmful products to the environment is discouraged.
• The price of goods increases, which will force producers to be more environmentally friendly.
• Consumption (output) of environmentally unfriendly goods is reduced.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: With the aid of a correctly labelled graph, briefly explain why it is advisable for oligopolies to sell at market price.
subQuestions.memoText:
Graph allocation (Max 4 marks):
• Labelling of axes (Price on Y-axis, Quantity on X-axis) = 1 mark
• Correct drawing and labelling of curves (kinked demand curve D1) = 2 marks
• E (kink point) clearly indicated = 1 mark

Explanation (Max 4 marks):
• When oligopolists sell at market price, they yield more income.
• Suppose an oligopolist is selling at a market price of R70 and 40 units of output are sold. Total revenue is R70 × 40 = R2 800.
• When a firm wants to increase profits by raising the price to R90, quantity demanded will fall to 10 units and total revenue would decrease to R90 × 10 = R900.
• If a firm wants to increase profits by reducing the price to R60, the quantity demanded will increase to 42 units, but total revenue would only be R60 × 42 = R2 520.
• Therefore, deviating from the market price (either upward or downward) reduces total revenue, so it is advisable for oligopolies to sell at the market price.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 4 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText: How does the government encourage producers to combat inflation?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per well-explained point). The government may encourage producers to combat inflation by:
• Paying cash grants to producers to encourage them to produce more goods and services to cater for excess demand.
• Providing subsidies on production to reduce the cost of production and enable producers to charge lower prices.
• Encouraging competition to promote the establishment of small businesses, thereby increasing aggregate supply.
• Improving the efficiency of parastatals that provide input services to reduce the cost of doing business (e.g. Eskom).
• Removing unnecessary laws and regulations to encourage producer efficiency.
• Maintaining exchange rate stability to ensure that producers import production inputs at a lower cost (e.g. oil and vehicle parts).
• Reducing corporate tax which will reduce cost, thereby encouraging production.
• Negotiating with countries for reduced tariffs on imported inputs which will reduce the cost of production.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)
(A maximum of 2 marks may be allocated for mere listing of facts/examples.)

subQuestions.questionText:
• Discuss the causes of market failure in detail. (26 marks)
• How effective has government spending been in addressing market failure? (10 marks) [40]
subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
• Introduction: Max 2
• Body – Main part: Max 26
• Body – Additional part: Max 10
• Conclusion: Max 2
TOTAL: 40

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):
Market failure occurs when market forces of demand and supply do not ensure the correct quantity of goods and services are produced to meet demand at the right price.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

BODY: MAIN PART (Max 26) – Discuss causes of market failure:

1. EXTERNALITIES
• These are known as spill-over effects to a third party which is not directly involved in the production process.
• As externalities in production and consumption often exist and output is usually based on private costs and benefits, this is a significant cause of market failure.

Negative externalities:
• Costs to third parties that are not included in the market price (e.g. pollution).
• The costs of negative externalities such as ill health are not paid by the producers.
• Harmful goods are often over-produced in the economy, which is not socially desirable.

Positive externalities:
• A positive externality occurs when a benefit accrues to a third party from the action or decision of another party (e.g. education).
• These goods are often under-produced by the market and government steps in to provide for the shortfall.
(A maximum of 4 marks will be allocated for graphical illustration.)

2. PUBLIC GOODS / MISSING MARKETS
• Markets can only form under certain conditions; when these conditions are absent, markets struggle to exist.
• Public goods are not provided for by the market mechanism because producers cannot withhold the goods for non-payment, and since there is often no way of measuring how much a person consumes, there is no basis to establish a market price.
• Examples include lighting, flood control, storm water drainage and lighthouses.
• Collective goods: parks, beaches and beach facilities, streets, pavements, roads, bridges, public transport, sewerage systems, waste removal, water reticulation and refuse removal.
• Community goods: defence, police services, prison services, streetlights.

3. MERIT GOODS AND DEMERIT GOODS
• Merit goods: highly desirable for the general welfare of the people of the country and are often not highly rated by the market. If people had to pay market prices for them, relatively little would be consumed.
• Demerit goods: items such as cigarettes, alcohol, and non-prescriptive drugs. In a free market economy, these goods are over-consumed.
• Government can ban their consumption or reduce it through taxation (e.g. excise duties) and by providing information about their harmful side effects.

4. IMPERFECT COMPETITION
• In market economies, competition is often impaired by power.
• Power often lies to a greater extent with producers than with consumers.
• Most businesses operate under conditions of imperfect competition that allow producers to restrict output, raise prices and produce where price exceeds marginal cost.

5. LACK OF INFORMATION
• Consumers, workers and entrepreneurs do not always have the necessary information at their disposal to make rational decisions.
• Consumers: do not have perfect information despite advances in technology.
• Workers: may be unaware of job opportunities outside their current employment.
• Entrepreneurs: may lack information about the costs, availability and productivity of some factors of production, and may operate on the basis of incorrect information.

6. IMMOBILITY OF THE FACTORS OF PRODUCTION
• Most markets do not adjust rapidly to changes in supply and demand.
• Labour: may take time to move into new occupations and geographically to meet changes in consumer demand.
• Physical capital: factory buildings and infrastructure such as telephone lines, bridges, rail links and airports are not moveable at will.
• This capital lasts for many years but cannot be moved to fit changes in demand.
• Technological applications change production methods (e.g. use of robots rather than labour in mines).
• It takes time for most industries to adapt to greater technological changes.
• Workers need to be flexible, upskilled and able to change employment, as well as work patterns.

7. IMPERFECT DISTRIBUTION OF INCOME AND WEALTH
• The most important shortcoming of market systems is that it is neutral on the issue of income distribution.
• If the initial distribution is unequal, the final distribution will be too.
• For this reason, it is often argued that the market fails.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10) – How effective has government spending been in addressing market failure?
Government spending is effective in addressing market failure by:
• Transferring income directly to the poor (e.g. child support grants, unemployment benefits) and thereby reducing income inequalities.
• Providing goods free of charge (e.g. community goods, education) and allowing access to basic needs to all citizens.
• Implementing employment creation programmes which will create jobs and improve skills for all types of labour (e.g. public works programme).
• Subsidising producers to encourage production of merit goods as they are beneficial to society.
• Spending on campaigns that will inform the public about policies and legislation that protects them against exploitation.
• Investing in infrastructure development such as roads, railways and communication networks, as the private sector finds these unprofitable or difficult to finance.
(Accept the negative evaluation of government spending.)
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):
Market failures can have devastating effects on the economy which require government to intervene to reduce their consequences.
(Accept any other correct relevant higher-order conclusion.)

subQuestions.questionText:
• Discuss in detail the benefits of tourism. (26 marks)
• Assess the impact of Covid-19 on the tourism sector. (10 marks) [40]
subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
• Introduction: Max 2
• Body – Main part: Max 26
• Body – Additional part: Max 10
• Conclusion: Max 2

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):
Tourism refers to activities of people travelling to and staying in places outside their usual environment for not more than one consecutive year and for different reasons.
(Accept any other correct relevant introduction.)

BODY: MAIN PART (Max 26) – Discuss the benefits of tourism:

1. HOUSEHOLDS
• Households may benefit from an increase in income and opportunities for employment and entrepreneurship.
• Individuals receive training through programmes established to promote tourism.
• Households are indirectly involved in tourism as employees in the hotel industry, financial institutions, etc.
• They benefit from improved infrastructure created for tourists which local people can also use.
• They acquire skills required by the tourism industry.
• Income earned is spent in their communities, contributing to the local economy.
• Entrepreneurs from households operate as tour guides.

2. BUSINESSES
• Formal sector activities are promoted through tourism (e.g. companies are tasked with building infrastructure such as hotels or roads).
• Tourism benefits local businesses and companies through an increase in expenditure on the goods and services offered.
• The informal sector benefits because of trading in traditional products such as crafts and arts.
• Banks employ more tellers, leading to higher employment.
• The business environment is stimulated in rural and urban areas, promoting entrepreneurial opportunities and assisting with BEE.
• Tourist destinations are developed through public and private partnerships (PPPs).

3. GOVERNMENT
• Government benefits because of income it receives from tourists.
• Tourism enables the government to advertise a country's tourism potential.
• Direct and indirect contributions to government revenue are made through levies on tourists, used:
  – To recover external costs (assists the host community in providing infrastructure).
  – To raise revenue (with the growth of tourism, many countries levy tourist taxes as a source of revenue).
• Income earned can be used to promote tourism in the country.
• The government is enabled to achieve its socio-economic objectives, including informal sector growth, BEE and SMME development.

4. INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT
• For any country to be regarded as a tourist destination, physical infrastructure has to be adequate and well maintained.
• The needs of large numbers of tourists for accommodation and infrastructure leads to the construction of hotels and improvement in existing infrastructure.
• Together with the private sector, the government has to develop and upgrade infrastructure to meet the demands and expectations of tourists.
• Locals and tourists benefit from the infrastructure.
• Tourists require social infrastructure (e.g. clinics and ambulances).

5. GROSS DOMESTIC PRODUCT (GDP)
• Travel and tourism contribute both directly and indirectly to GDP.
• Direct contribution: internal spending of travel and tourism by residents and non-residents for business and leisure (e.g. spending on accommodation, food, retail, transport, destination services, and public sector spending directly linked to visitors).
• Indirect contribution: purchases from suppliers of goods and services by sectors dealing directly with tourists (e.g. cleaning services for hotels, fuel and catering services for airlines, IT services for travel agents).

6. EMPLOYMENT
The tourism sector is a large generator of jobs because:
• Tourism is labour-intensive (lowest rate of investment to employment creation).
• Tourism employs many skills (accountants, hairdressers, tour guides, etc.).
• Tourism can provide immediate employment if properly organised and focused.
• Tourism provides entrepreneurial opportunities (informal sector enterprises, craft and fruit vendors, pavement vendors, chair rentals, etc.).

7. POVERTY ALLEVIATION
• Tourism brings development to the poor in rural areas.
• Tourism offers opportunities to diversify sources of income for poor people:
  – Allowing them a stake (e.g. operating small-scale tourism businesses around community assets and establishing SMMEs).
  – Empowering them (e.g. exploiting opportunities for on-the-job and other training).
  – Creating partnerships with mainstream tourism businesses supplying goods and services.
• Consider inputs related to the benefits of international tourists.
